What’s happening In the last 48 hours, several European governments have raised the level of alarm on the Russian threat, transforming scenarios so far confined to military planning into public messages. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has … Written by: Jack Williams Published on: September 20, 2026 In the last 48 hours, several European governments have raised the level of alarm on the Russian threat, transforming scenarios so far confined to military planning into public messages. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that Moscow could attempt drone or missile attacks against countries that support Ukraine, then try to present them as accidents. In France, President Emmanuel Macron brought together intelligence and political leaders, ordering a strengthening of the protection of critical infrastructures and the defense industry. Faced with the deterioration of the international situation, we meet the chefs of the parties represented in Parliament to make the point. https://t.co/r7lO9fB6aL — Emmanuel Macron (@EmmanuelMacron) September 18, 2026 Estonia and Lithuania are instead updating their plans for broader crisis scenarios: Tallinn is evaluating the possible closure of the border in the event of a general Russian mobilization, while Vilnius has set up evacuation routes towards Poland. Even neutral Switzerland has raised the alert level by adapting a strategy and a new defensive policy “in response to the deteriorated security situation”. In response to the deteriorating security situation, 🇨🇭 has three objectives: strengthen resilience, improve protection and enhance defense capabilities. The Federal Council has adopted Switzerland’s Security Policy Strategy 2026. https://t.co/VzEujnJzNr @vbs_ddps — Swiss Federal Government (@SwissGov) September 18, 2026 The Belarusian military exercises near the Polish and Lithuanian borders and the Suwałki Corridor, as well as the recent violations of NATO airspace, contribute to making the situation more tense. It does not mean that a Russian attack is considered imminent, but it signals a substantial change: European governments are openly preparing populations and institutions for scenarios of sabotage, incursions and possible military escalation that until recently remained mostly on paper. What’s happening THE’ Economist claims that Vladimir Putin, finding himself in a situation of growing military stalemate in Ukraine, decided to react not by seeking a compromise, but by increasing the level of conflict. According to sources close to the Kremlin cited by the weekly, the choice would have been made during the summer. In the Russian elite, writes the Economist the perception is growing that the simple fact of having taken so long already represents a failure, regardless of the final outcome. In response, Moscow could try to change the situation by raising the level of the war, in Ukraine but above all through hybrid operations and sabotage against the European countries that support it. The logic attributed to Putin is that of a system in which showing weakness is more dangerous than increasing violence. Russia can strike NATO without declaring war on it War could therefore arrive in Europe without being declared. This is the fear that is growing at European and NATO leaders: not so much a conventional invasion of an Alliance country, but rather limited and ambiguous attacks, serious enough to cause damage but designed to leave open the question: is it really a Russian attack or an accident? In recent months, Europe has already seen sabotage, fires, cyber operations, drone overflights and airspace violations attributed or suspected to be linked to Russia. In September, an Italian fighter on a NATO mission shot down a drone in Lithuania that had entered from Belarus and was considered potentially explosive. The alarm was formulated more clearly by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Citing undisclosed intelligence information, he said Moscow could strike countries supporting Kiev with drones or missiles, later describing the incidents as “accidental.” The goal, according to Tusk, would be to test the allies’ willingness to apply Article 5 of NATO, the principle according to which an attack against one member state is an attack against all. Propaganda At the same time, influence activity aimed at influencing public opinion and Western political decisions is increasing. According to the American study center Institute for the Study of War, Moscow would conduct a series of cognitive and information campaigns coordinated with the “kinetic” ones against European states. In a recently published report, the institute brings together a long series of episodes ranging from attempts to sabotage railways, fires against defense companies, cyberattacks, activities against submarine cables, violations of NATO airspace and alleged plans against executives of the European military industry. Next to a “cognitive warfare” infrastructure would tend to influence the perceptions, will and decisions of its adversaries thanks to partnerships between Russian state media and foreign newspapers, journalism training programs financed or managed by the Russian state and the cultural centers known as “Russian House” through which Moscow exercises cultural diplomacy and, according to the interpretation of the ISW, projects its influence abroad. The goal would be much more ambitious than simply spreading propaganda on a daily basis. In short, there are not enough signs to say that Russia is preparing to invade a NATO country in the coming weeks, but European governments are preparing for a more aggressive phase of hybrid warfare. https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/n.text: Finland’s ambassador to Australia, Arto Haapea: ‘I think people are just looking for good news.’ Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Finland’s ambassador to Australia, Arto Haapea: ‘I think people are just looking for good news.’ Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/The Guardian Social media ‘We were quite surprised’: Finland’s embassy in Australia goes viral with staff training day post on Instagram After a promotion for a ‘Finnish Dinner Date’ went ‘a bit viral’, the Canberra envoy’s next post became an unlikely social media hit Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Josh Butler Wed 11 Nov 2026 09.00 EST Last modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 15.45 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The embassy of Finland in Canberra was temporarily closed on Tuesday. Millions of people across the world were, it turns out, quite upset by this. A day later, with the flourish of a ribbon-cutting ceremony, the embassy reopened its doors – having garnered many millions of views on its videos, spurred memes seen by millions more and social media attention across the globe, all unexpectedly from an innocuous Instagram post about a staff training day. “We were all having a nice planning day, then someone said: ‘Oh my goodness, it’s gone completely viral,’” Arto Haapea, Finland’s ambassador to Australia, told Guardian Australia. The Finnish embassy, nestled in leafy Yarralumla in Canberra’s diplomatic zone just a stone’s throw from Parliament House, isn’t exactly a tourist hotspot in the nation’s capital. Flanked by the embassies of Estonia, Singapore, Mexico and Samoa, the sleek building – all grey panelling and glass – looks more like a bank or an office block than the genesis of a bizarre social media sensation stretching from Europe and the US to the centre of Australian politics. View image in fullscreen Photograph: Instagram/Finland in Australia “The embassy of Finland in Canberra will be temporarily closed on Tuesday, 10 November 2026. Regular hours will resume on Wednesday, 11 November,” @FinlandInAustralia posted on Monday, with text over video of the northern lights glowing an eerie green. Last week, the embassy’s other Instagram videos were getting like counts in the dozens or low hundreds. The post about the building’s opening hours has, as of time of writing, been liked 622,000 times, shared 405,000 times, and been seen by up to 10 million people worldwide. View image in fullscreen Photograph: Instagram/Finland in Australia How it got picked up by Instagram’s social media algorithm, and supercharged to be seen across the world, is likely something to do with the embassy’s previous video ; Haapea promoting a competition to fly single people from around the world to Helsinki for a “Finnish Dinner Date”. The dinner date video also “went a bit viral”, Haapea said, getting 8m views and 163,000 likes. “We were quite surprised by that,” the ambassador said. Haapea said his team hadn’t had time to do any deep analysis of why these two clips went unexpectedly viral, but he theorised that the post with the opening hours “happened to ride on the same algorithm” as the dinner date, getting even more views, and attracting influencers, companies and brands around the world to make their own videos. View image in fullscreen Photograph: Instagram/Finland in Australia “POV you’re trying to enter the Embassy of Finland in Canberra but it’s 10th of November,” posted @j.ackdale, knocking on a locked door. That has 604,000 likes on Instagram at the time of writing. “Me, all the way from Muscat, trying to get answers about the Finnish embassy in Canberra,” posted @sand_and_heels from Oman. All aboard the TrainTok trend: spotters and staff boost rail content online Read more “I’m flying over 300 people from Finland to Australia. Hopefully the Embassy of Finland in Canberra is open today,” posted Finnish pilot @juusojelmer, to 88,000 likes. That included Finnish politicians and ambassadors around the world, many of whom posted their own jokes, calling their colleagues or reassuring Finns in various countries that their embassies remained open. Haapea said even Finland’s foreign minister was keen to chat. View image in fullscreen The Finland embassy in Yarralumla, Canberra. Photograph: Paul Kingsley/Alamy “We were done with the planning day and did a sauna with the team, and the foreign minister wanted to call about the planning day,” he said, as they filmed a video together – Haapea fresh from the sauna – promising that normal functions of the embassy would resume the next day. On Wednesday, Canberrans from politicians to radio hosts and journalists visited the embassy, making their own social media clips live from the scene, while ordinary people tried knocking on the door or chatting to Finnish staff. A lighthearted video with a grand reopening , complete with ribbon-cutting ceremony, had to come next, Haapea said. “We thank the international community for your fascinating interest,” the embassy posted. As to why the interest in the first place? The ambassador said he’s still not sure. “I think people are just looking for good news, to take their minds off all the craziness in the world. With the algorithm, and people who are good at making memes, all it took was a few big influencers to make a meme about it,” Haapea said.
